draft.title: Threats to the Great Barrier Reef
card: The Great Barrier Reef is a huge system of coral reefs off the Queensland coast. It faces several threats at once, and some are made worse by human activity.
Warming seas
as the climate warms, so does the ocean. Hotter water stresses corals and can harm the reef across large areas.
Farm runoff
rain washes soil and fertiliser from farms into rivers and out to sea. The extra nutrients and cloudy water harm corals and can help crown-of-thorns starfish numbers grow.
Starfish and cyclones
crown-of-thorns starfish eat living coral. Stronger cyclones can break reef structures with waves and flood the water with runoff.
draft.remember: The reef faces threats from warming seas, farm runoff, crown-of-thorns starfish and stronger cyclones.

a.q: Fertiliser from sugar cane farms in Queensland washes down a river after heavy rain and reaches the sea near the reef. Which threat is this?
opts: Farm runoff
Warming seas
Crown-of-thorns starfish
Stronger cyclones
a.why: Soil and fertiliser carried from farmland by rain and rivers is farm runoff. Cyclones can cause heavy rain, but the threat here is the material washed off the land, not the storm.
a.clue: Think about where the fertiliser comes from and how it gets to the sea.

b.q: Divers at a reef near Cairns find large patches of coral with their living tissue eaten away, and many starfish with spines on the coral. Which threat is the most likely cause?
opts: Crown-of-thorns starfish feeding on the coral
Stronger cyclones breaking the coral with waves
Warming seas stressing the coral across the reef
Soil in the water blocking light from the coral
b.why: Crown-of-thorns starfish eat living coral, and the divers found them on the damaged patches. Cyclones break reef structures with waves, so they would not leave tissue eaten away by feeding animals.
b.clue: What was found on the coral, and what does it do to coral?

b.best: Crown-of-thorns starfish feeding on the coral

problems.detail: The stem says divers found 'many starfish' on the coral, and only one option mentions starfish. A student can match the word without knowing what crown-of-thorns starfish do to coral.

proposal.remember: Warming seas, farm runoff, starfish and cyclones all harm the reef, and some can make others worse.

a.q: Fertiliser from sugar cane farms in Queensland washes down a river after heavy rain and reaches the sea near the reef. Which threat is this?
opts: Farm runoff
Warming seas
Crown-of-thorns starfish
Stronger cyclones
a.why: Soil and fertiliser carried from farmland by rain and rivers is farm runoff. Cyclones can cause heavy rain, but the threat here is the material washed off the land, not the storm.
a.clue: Think about where the fertiliser comes from and how it gets to the sea.

b.q: After a wet year, rivers carry extra fertiliser to a reef near Mackay. Later, divers find more coral with its living tissue eaten away. What best explains the link?
opts: Nutrients helped crown-of-thorns starfish numbers grow
Fertiliser warmed the sea water around the coral
Cloudy water made cyclones stronger over the reef
Nutrients made the coral grow too fast and die
b.why: Extra nutrients from farm runoff can help crown-of-thorns starfish numbers grow, and these starfish eat living coral. Warming seas come from a warming climate, not from fertiliser, so that option mixes up two separate threats.
b.clue: Which threat eats living coral, and what helps it spread?
